say.text: Before I teach anything, try this cold. It is meant to be a bit hard.

A 12-day-old is brought in with blue lips and tongue, worse on crying. There is a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left mid to upper sternal border, and you cannot hear a pulmonary component of S2.
Which single lesion do you bet on?

choices.label: An innocent flow murmur; he is just cold
No idea, give me a clue

say.text: Transposition is a tempting pick because any cyanotic baby makes you think of it. But it ignores your best clues: a harsh ejection murmur and an inaudible pulmonary S2 are the described TOF findings.
Take one more look with that in mind.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look. Anchor on the murmur and the pulmonary S2 together, not on the colour alone.

say.text: An innocent murmur is tempting in a newborn. But a harsh ejection murmur with an inaudible pulmonary S2 is not innocent, and a baby with blue lips is cyanotic.
Take one more look with that in mind.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look. Anchor on the murmur and the pulmonary S2 together, not on the colour alone.

say.text: Clue: think of the commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease. Its murmur is a harsh systolic ejection murmur, and the pulmonary component of S2 is usually inaudible.
Second attempt, with the clue: the commonest cyanotic lesion, harsh ejection murmur, quiet pulmonary S2.
Which lesion?

choices.label: An innocent flow murmur; he is just cold

say.text: It was Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), and missing it on a first look is normal. The harsh ejection murmur and the usually inaudible pulmonary S2 are its signature.
Yes, Tetralogy of Fallot. The harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left mid to upper sternal border and the usually inaudible pulmonary S2 are the clues.
Now a harder one you have not been taught. Make a best guess.
What makes this baby blue?

choices.label: Blood shunts toward the aorta and bypasses the lungs
The lungs are flooded with too much blood
The heart muscle is too weak to pump blood

say.text: Your attempt hits the mechanism. With significant RVOT obstruction, most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
The name of the lesion tells you its four parts: a large anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Flooded lungs is tempting, because many heart lesions send too much blood to the lungs. Here that misses the key point: with significant RVOT obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
The lesion has four parts: a large anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember this gap: the obstruction at the outflow is what steers blood away from the lungs.

say.text: A weak pump is tempting, because a failing heart looks unwell. But it misses the real cause: with significant RVOT obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
The lesion has four parts: a large anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.

say.text: Last bet. This lesion is how common among cyanotic congenital heart diseases, and how does it most often present?

choices.label: Commonest cyanotic CHD, most often a cyanotic neonate
A rare cyanotic lesion, so it is unlikely in a neonate
Commonest cyanotic CHD, but it only shows up at school age

say.text: Hint: the lesion behind your baby's findings has a big title. It is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, and the baby on your couch is 12 days old.
Second try, with the hint.
Where does it rank, and how does it most often present?

choices.label: Commonest cyanotic CHD, most often a cyanotic neonate
A rare cyanotic lesion, so it is unlikely in a neonate
Commonest cyanotic CHD, but it only shows up at school age

say.text: Here is the answer. TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, and it most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate, just like your patient.
Right. TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, and it most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate.

sure_note.text: Confident and correct, so lock it in: most common cyanotic CHD, usually a cyanotic neonate.

say.text: Notice what your first guesses missed: the obstruction at the RVOT steers blood away from the lungs. The severity of that obstruction sets how the child presents.
Next, let us pin down the four parts properly.
